g11-economics-ue2-t1.overview: Markets differ in how many sellers compete, what they trade and how freely information flows. This lesson reviews the four market structures and locates the perfectly competitive firm as a price taker and the monopolist as a price maker.
objectives: Define a market and the meaning of market structure
State the criteria used to distinguish market structures
List the four popular types of market structures
Order market structures from most to least competitive
Distinguish between price taker and price maker firms
g11-economics-ue2-t1.simple: A market is a mechanism by which the exchange of goods and services takes place when buyers and sellers are in contact, either directly or through mediating agents or institutions. Market structure refers to how industries are classified and differentiated based on their degree and nature of competition for goods and services. The main criteria for distinguishing structures are the number and size of firms and consumers, the type of goods and services being traded, and the degree to which information can flow freely. The four popular types are perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly and pure monopoly. From most to least competitive the order is exactly that: perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, pure monopoly. Under perfect competition every small firm is a price taker while the industry is the price maker; under monopoly the single firm is itself a price maker.
g11-economics-ue2-t1.detailed:
What a market is. In general, a market is a mechanism by which the exchange of goods and services takes place as a result of buyers and sellers being in contact with one another, either directly or through mediating agents or institutions. The contact may be a face-to-face sale in a village grain market or a trade arranged through brokers or other institutions; what matters is that buyers and sellers are brought together so exchange can occur.

What market structure means. Market structure refers to how different industries are classified and differentiated based on their degree and nature of competition for goods and services. Market structure makes it easier to understand the characteristics of diverse markets. The main criteria by which one can distinguish between different market structures are: the number and size of firms and consumers in the market, the type of goods and services being traded, and the degree to which information can flow freely.

The four popular structures. The four popular types of market structures include perfect competition, oligopoly market, monopoly market and monopolistic competition. The correct sequence of the market structure from most to least competitive is: perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, and pure monopoly. Perfect competition has very many small sellers of a homogeneous (identical) product; monopolistic competition has many sellers whose products are differentiated; oligopoly is dominated by a few large, mutually interdependent sellers; and pure monopoly has a single seller of a good or service with no close substitutes and entry by rivals that is prohibitively difficult.

Price takers and price makers. In a perfectly competitive market each individual firm is insignificant compared with the market size and supplies a product no different from the products of other firms, so it cannot determine the price. Prices are determined by the interaction of all consumers and producers, that is, by the forces of demand and supply, and every firm assumes this price as given. Such a firm is a price taker, while the industry as a whole is the price maker. A monopoly stands at the opposite end: it does not take the market price as given but determines its own price, selecting from its demand curve the price matching the profit-maximizing quantity. A firm that sets price from its output decision is a price setter and is said to possess monopoly power.

Homogeneous products, differentiated products and collusion. Products are homogeneous when units are identical, as with basic farm crops, so no buyer prefers one seller to another. Products are differentiated when buyers perceive them as distinctive in style, brand, location or image, even when the difference rests on advertising rather than on the good itself. Among the few firms of an oligopoly, rivals may either collude by raising agreements, explicit or implicit, to fix price and output, or else compete independently; the pair of possibilities called collusion and non-collusion is a key concept used throughout this unit.

keyTerms.def: A mechanism by which the exchange of goods and services takes place as a result of buyers and sellers being in contact, directly or through mediating agents or institutions.
How industries are classified and differentiated based on the degree and nature of competition for goods and services.
The most competitive structure: many small sellers of a homogeneous product, each taking the market price as given.
The least competitive structure: a single seller with no close substitutes and entry by potential rivals prohibitively difficult.
A firm that assumes the market-determined price as given and cannot influence it; every perfectly competitive firm is a price taker.
A firm or industry that determines price; the perfectly competitive industry is the price maker, and a monopolist sets its own price as a price setter.
Identical units of a product for which buyers have no preference among sellers, such as basic farm crops.
Products regarded by buyers as distinctive in style, brand, location or perception, giving each seller some monopoly power.

workedExamples.problem: Ten thousand small farmers each sell identical white teff at one central terminal market where the day's price is announced to all. Classify this market.
workedExamples.given: Very many small sellers, identical (homogeneous) product, and a single ruling price that no farmer can change alone.
workedExamples.formula: Classification rule: many small sellers + homogeneous product + price taking = perfect competition.
workedExamples.substitution: Each farmer supplies an insignificant share of total market output, so no farmer can move the price.
workedExamples.calculation: The market matches perfect competition: the industry sets the price through demand and supply and each farmer is a price taker.
workedExamples.answer: A perfectly competitive market; each farmer is a price taker and the industry is the price maker.

workedExamples.problem: Three large companies dominate a national beer market, and each company watches the others closely before changing price or advertising. Classify this market.
workedExamples.given: A few large sellers whose actions strongly affect one another.
workedExamples.formula: Classification rule: few large interdependent sellers = oligopoly, whether products are homogeneous or differentiated.
workedExamples.substitution: Each company's price and advertising decisions depend on the expected reactions of the other two.
workedExamples.calculation: The relationship of mutual dependence among a few dominant sellers is the defining feature of oligopoly.
workedExamples.answer: An oligopoly market with strategic interdependence among the few firms.

workedExamples.problem: A foreign company holds the only patent for a new medicine, so no other firm can legally produce or import a close substitute for years. Classify this market and identify the firm's price role.
workedExamples.given: One seller; no close substitutes; entry blocked by the patent right.
workedExamples.formula: Classification rule: single seller + no close substitutes + blocked entry = pure monopoly.
workedExamples.substitution: The firm does not take any market price as given; it picks the price matching its chosen output from its demand curve.
workedExamples.calculation: Since it sets price from its output decision, the firm is a price setter with monopoly power.
workedExamples.answer: A pure monopoly; the firm is a price maker (price setter) rather than a price taker.

workedExamples.problem: A street has many small restaurants, each serving dishes and flavours that differ from the others, yet new restaurants enter freely. Classify this market.
workedExamples.given: Many sellers, distinctive (differentiated) products, easy entry.
workedExamples.formula: Classification rule: many sellers + differentiated products = monopolistic competition.
workedExamples.substitution: Each restaurant has a mini-monopoly over its own style of food but faces keen competition from close substitutes.
workedExamples.calculation: The mixture of product distinctiveness and tough rivalry matches monopolistic competition, which lies between monopoly and perfect competition.
workedExamples.answer: A monopolistically competitive market.

commonMistakes: Listing oligopoly or monopoly before monopolistic competition when ordering structures by competitiveness.
Confusing the purpose of market structure: it classifies industries by degree and nature of competition, not by geography alone.
Forgetting that the number and size of firms, the type of goods traded and the free flow of information are the distinguishing criteria.
Calling a perfectly competitive firm a price maker instead of a price taker.
Saying the single competitive firm, not the industry, determines the market price.
Believing differentiated products must differ physically; advertising and brand image can create perceived differences.
Assuming pure monopoly and oligopoly are the same because both involve market power; monopoly has one seller, oligopoly a few.
applications: Classify any market you visit by asking three questions: how many sellers are there, are products identical or distinctive, and how easily can new firms enter?
Explain why many small grain traders in a surplus teff market all quote nearly the same price rather than each setting a different price.
Use the price taker and price maker distinction to explain why one shop cannot raise the local price of a standard soap brand above other shops.
Discuss why a firm holding a patent on a medicine behaves like a price maker until the patent expires.
Predict which structure fits Ethiopian mobile telecommunication or cement markets by counting the dominant sellers and observing their interdependence.
Prepare for later lessons: the same four structures will now be examined one by one, starting with perfect competition.
g11-economics-ue2-t1.summary: A market is the mechanism through which buyers and sellers in contact exchange goods and services, and market structure classifies industries by the degree and nature of competition using the number and size of participants, the type of product and the flow of information. The four structures run from most to least competitive as perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly and pure monopoly. Perfectly competitive firms are price takers while the industry is the price maker; a monopolist sets its own price as a price setter.

options: Perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, pure monopoly
Pure monopoly, oligopoly, monopolistic competition, perfect competition
Oligopoly, perfect competition, pure monopoly, monopolistic competition
Monopolistic competition, perfect competition, oligopoly, pure monopoly
questions.explanation: The textbook sequence from most to least competitive is perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, then pure monopoly.

questions.q: Market structure refers to how industries are classified based on the degree and nature of competition.
questions.explanation: This is the textbook definition of market structure.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the main criteria for distinguishing market structures?
options: The number and size of firms and consumers
The type of goods and services being traded
The degree to which information can flow freely
The colour of the firms' buildings
questions.explanation: The criteria are the number and size of participants, the type of goods and services, and the free flow of information.

questions.q: What do we call a firm that assumes the market-determined price as given?
questions.answer: price taker|price-taker
questions.explanation: Every perfectly competitive firm takes the market price as given, so it is a price taker.

questions.q: In a perfectly competitive market, the price maker is:
options: The largest firm in the industry
questions.explanation: Prices are determined by the interaction of all consumers and producers in the industry, so the industry is the price maker while each firm is a price taker.

questions.q: A monopoly firm need not worry about other firms entering its market because entry by potential rivals is prohibitively difficult.
questions.explanation: The textbook states that in monopoly entry by potential rivals is prohibitively difficult, so the monopolist has the market to itself.

questions.q: Explain the difference between homogeneous and differentiated products.
questions.answer: homogeneous products are identical while differentiated products are seen as distinct in style, brand or perception|identical products versus products considered different by buyers
questions.explanation: Homogeneous products, such as basic farm crops, are identical; differentiated products are distinctive in style, flavour, location or image, sometimes only because of advertising.

questions.q: Which market structure is made up of a few large, mutually interdependent sellers?
questions.answer: oligopoly
questions.explanation: Oligopoly is dominated by a few large sellers whose actions affect one another.

questions.q: A firm that sets or picks price based on its output decision is called a:
questions.explanation: A firm that sets price from its output decision is a price setter and possesses monopoly power.

questions.q: Arrange the four market structures starting from the most competitive. Which option comes first in the correct order?
questions.explanation: The order is: perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, pure monopoly; so perfect competition starts the sequence.

g11-economics-ue2-t2.overview: In perfect competition many small sellers of an identical product take the price the market sets. This lesson derives the firm's revenue and cost curves, its short-run and long-run equilibrium, its supply curve and its shutdown decision.
objectives: Explain why a perfectly competitive firm is a price taker with a horizontal demand curve
Show that price, average revenue and marginal revenue are all equal for the firm
Determine short-run equilibrium using the TR-TC and MR-MC approaches
Identify the price and output levels at which firms earn profits, break even or incur losses
Derive the short-run supply curve and state the long-run equilibrium condition
g11-economics-ue2-t2.simple: Under perfect competition the price is fixed by the interaction of market demand and supply, so every firm takes that price as given. The firm's demand curve is horizontal and price equals both average revenue and marginal revenue (P = AR = MR). Total revenue rises as a straight line whose slope is the price. In the short run the firm maximizes profit where the gap between total revenue and total cost is largest, which is also where marginal revenue equals marginal cost with marginal cost rising. Depending on price compared with average cost, the firm may earn profit, zero profit or a loss. If price still covers average variable cost it keeps producing; below the shutdown point it stops. The short-run supply curve is the part of the marginal cost curve above average variable cost. In the long run entry and exit drive price to the minimum of long-run average cost.
g11-economics-ue2-t2.detailed:
The firm as a price taker. The characteristics of perfect competition imply that every firm is insignificant compared with the market size, and since its product is in no way different from the products of other firms, each individual firm cannot determine prices. The price is determined by the interaction of all consumers and producers in the market, that is, by demand and supply. Every firm then assumes this price as given and decides its output accordingly. Firms are therefore price takers and the industry is the price maker. Each firm faces a horizontal demand curve: it can sell whatever quantity it wishes at the market price, which means its demand for the product is perfectly elastic.

Revenue of the firm. Total revenue is price times quantity, TR = P x Q. Since the price is constant, the total revenue curve is a straight line whose slope equals the price. Average revenue is TR divided by Q, which is exactly the price, and marginal revenue is the change in TR from selling one more unit, which also equals the price. Hence for the perfectly competitive firm P = AR = DD = MR. Average cost behaves typically: the ATC curve is U-shaped, falling at first and then rising, while the marginal cost curve falls briefly and then rises because of diminishing marginal returns. When average cost declines, MC is less than AC; when average cost rises, MC is greater than AC; and when average cost is at its minimum, MC equals AC.

Short-run equilibrium: the TR-TC approach. The short run is a period in which the quantity of at least one input is fixed, while the long run is a period in which all inputs can be varied; there is no fixed calendar time separating them. Profit is total revenue minus total cost. Using the total approach, the firm is in equilibrium at the output where profit is maximum, that is, where the gap of total revenue over total cost is largest. Total revenue rises as the firm sells more, and total cost also rises but with curvature, so the vertical distance between them is greatest at a single output level.

Short-run equilibrium: the MR-MC approach. Marginal revenue shows the additional revenue from selling one more unit and is constant at the price for a competitive firm, while marginal cost is the change in TC per change in output. The first condition for equilibrium is MR - MC = 0, that is, MR = MC. This condition alone is not sufficient, because it can hold at points where the firm is not in equilibrium. The second condition requires that MC be rising at the intersection, so the MC must cut the MR curve from below: the slope of MC must be steeper than the slope of MR. Since marginal revenue equals price, the profit-maximizing rule can also be written as P = MC.

Profit, break-even and loss. Whether producing where MR = MC yields an actual economic profit depends on price compared with average total cost. If price is greater than average cost at the chosen quantity, the firm earns profits. If price exactly equals average cost, which occurs at the minimum point of the AC curve, the firm earns zero profits. If price is less than average cost, the firm incurs losses. A loss-making firm does not automatically shut down: shutting down reduces variable costs to zero, but in the short run fixed costs have already been paid, so producing zero still means losing the fixed costs.

The shutdown decision and short-run supply. If price falls in the zone between the shutdown point and the zero-profit (break-even) point, the firm makes losses but continues to operate in the short run because it covers its variable costs. If price falls below the shutdown point, the firm shuts down immediately since it does not even cover variable costs. The shutdown point is the intersection of the average variable cost curve and the marginal cost curve. Because the firm will supply output at any price at or above minimum average variable cost, the short-run supply curve of a perfectly competitive firm is that portion of the marginal cost curve lying above the average variable cost curve. The industry's short-run supply curve is obtained by the lateral summation of the firms' short-run marginal cost curves above AVC, and it always slopes upward because those MC curves slope upward.

Long-run equilibrium. The long run allows any change to production, including the entry and exit of firms. If existing firms make pure economic profits, new firms enter because returns in the industry are higher than elsewhere; supply shifts to the right and price falls. If firms make economic losses that cannot be eliminated, they leave the market; supply falls and price rises. Adjustment continues until returns in the industry equal returns elsewhere and no entry or exit incentive remains. In the long run the firm adjusts its plant to produce at the minimum point of its long-run average cost curve, which is tangential to the horizontal demand curve, and the firm just earns normal profits. The long-run equilibrium condition is LMC = LAC = P, and at the minimum of LAC the full chain SMC = LMC = SAC = LAC = P = MR holds, the minima of LAC and SAC coinciding.

keyTerms.def: A perfectly competitive firm that accepts the market-determined price and can sell any quantity at that price.
Price times quantity sold; for a price-taking firm it plots as a straight line from the origin whose slope is the price.
Total revenue divided by quantity; equal to price and to the firm's demand curve in perfect competition.
The change in total revenue from selling one more unit; equal to price for a perfectly competitive firm.
The change in total cost from producing one more unit; derived from variable costs and rising beyond low output levels.
The output where profit is greatest: MR = MC with marginal cost rising, or the largest gap of total revenue over total cost.
The price-output position where price equals minimum average cost and the firm earns zero (normal) profit.
The intersection of marginal cost with average variable cost; at any price below it the firm stops producing even in the short run.

workedExamples.problem: A perfectly competitive firm has the cost function C = Q^2 + 20Q + 700 and the equilibrium price is Birr 100. Find the profit-maximizing output and the maximum profit.
workedExamples.given: Cost C = Q^2 + 20Q + 700; market price P = Birr 100, so MR = 100.
workedExamples.formula: Profit maximizing rule: P = MC; then profit = TR - TC = P x Q - C.
workedExamples.substitution: MC = change in C per change in Q = 2Q + 20. Set P = MC: 100 = 2Q + 20, so 2Q = 80.
workedExamples.answer: The profit-maximizing output is 40 units and the maximum profit is Birr 900, which is positive because P = 100 exceeds average cost (3100/40 = 77.5).

workedExamples.problem: At a market price of Birr 12 a firm's total costs for outputs 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 units are Birr 5, 9, 16, 26 and 40. Use the TR-TC approach to find its best output.
workedExamples.given: P = Birr 12; TC rises as Birr 5, 9, 16, 26, 40 for Q = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
workedExamples.formula: TR = P x Q; profit = TR - TC; choose the output with the largest gap of TR over TC.
workedExamples.substitution: TR = Birr 0, 12, 24, 36, 48. Profits = TR - TC = Birr -5, 3, 8, 10, 8.
workedExamples.calculation: Profit rises to a maximum of Birr 10 at Q = 3, then falls to Birr 8 at Q = 4 because the fourth unit adds MC of Birr 14, which exceeds MR = 12.
workedExamples.answer: Produce 3 units; profit is Birr 10. Checks also satisfy MR = MC where MC (Birr 10 for the third unit) below MR reinforces the same choice.

workedExamples.problem: A firm's profit-maximizing price is Birr 18. At that output its minimum average variable cost is Birr 15 and its average total cost is Birr 22. Should the firm operate or shut down?
workedExamples.given: P = Birr 18; minimum AVC = Birr 15; ATC at that output = Birr 22.
workedExamples.formula: Decision rule: operate if the shutdown point price (min AVC) is less than or equal to P, even when P < ATC.
workedExamples.substitution: P = 18 lies between 15 (min AVC) and 22 (ATC).
workedExamples.calculation: Revenue covers all variable costs and part of the fixed cost, so the loss from producing (18 - 22) is smaller than the loss from shutting down (the whole fixed cost).
workedExamples.answer: Continue operating in the short run: the firm is above its shutdown point even though it incurs a loss below the break-even point.

workedExamples.problem: Many small poultry farms around a town currently earn economic profits. Explain the long-run adjustment in this perfectly competitive market.
workedExamples.given: Positive economic profits attract entrants because returns exceed what can be earned elsewhere.
workedExamples.formula: Long-run mechanism: entry shifts industry supply right, price falls until P = minimum LAC.
workedExamples.substitution: New farms increase the quantity supplied at every price, so the market supply curve shifts rightward.
workedExamples.calculation: Price falls until each farm earns exactly normal profit at the minimum of its long-run average cost curve, where LMC = LAC = P.
workedExamples.answer: Entry continues until profits are competed away; in long-run equilibrium farms earn normal profits and SMC = LMC = SAC = LAC = P = MR.

commonMistakes: Drawing the firm's demand curve downward-sloping; under perfect competition the individual firm's demand curve is horizontal while the market demand curve slopes down.
Treating MR = MC alone as sufficient; the second condition requires MC to cut MR from below (MC rising at the intersection).
Assuming that producing where MR = MC always guarantees positive profit; the same rule also identifies the loss-minimizing output.
Claiming a loss-making firm should always shut down at once; it may keep operating when price still covers average variable cost.
Placing the shutdown point at minimum average total cost instead of at minimum average variable cost.
Saying the perfectly competitive firm makes the price; it is a price taker and only the industry is the price maker.
Treating the short run and the long run as fixed calendar periods; the distinction varies from one industry to another.
applications: In a grain market where thousands of traders sell identical teff, a farmer plans output knowing the ruling price cannot be influenced by him.
A baker selling standard loaves at the neighbourhood fixed price decides the daily number of loaves where marginal cost rises to the price.
An avocado cutter stops supplying when the market price falls below her minimum average variable cost, the shutdown point.
Market analysts obtain the industry supply curve by summing the supply curves of many small farms whose marginal costs rise with output.
High profits in poultry raising attract new entrants, raising supply and driving the price down to minimum long-run average cost.
Understanding P = AR = MR explains why a single vendour cannot sell the same product at a different price than other sellers in the market.
g11-economics-ue2-t2.summary: A perfectly competitive firm is a price taker facing a horizontal demand curve where P = AR = MR, and its straight-line total revenue curve has slope equal to the price. Short-run equilibrium requires MR = MC with MC rising (equivalently P = MC); depending on price versus average cost the firm earns profit, normal profit or a loss, and it shuts down only when price falls below the minimum of average variable cost. In the long run entry and exit push price to the minimum of long-run average cost, where firms earn just normal profit and SMC = LMC = SAC = LAC = P = MR.

questions.q: In a perfectly competitive market the demand curve facing an individual firm is:
questions.explanation: The firm can sell whatever quantity it wishes at the market price, so its demand curve is horizontal and perfectly elastic.

questions.q: For a perfectly competitive firm, price, average revenue, marginal revenue and the demand curve are all equal.
questions.explanation: The textbook gives the chain P = AR = DD = MR for the competitive firm.

questions.q: Why is the total revenue curve of a perfectly competitive firm a straight line?
options: Because demand falls as output rises
questions.explanation: TR = P x Q, and the constant market price makes the TR curve a straight line whose slope equals the price.

questions.q: The second condition for short-run equilibrium of the firm is that:
options: MC must cut the MR curve from below (MC rising)
questions.explanation: MR = MC alone is not sufficient; MC must be rising, so its slope is steeper than the slope of MR.

questions.q: At which point of the average cost curve does a firm earn exactly zero profit?
questions.answer: minimum point of the AC curve|minimum AC|minimum of average cost
questions.explanation: When price equals average cost at its minimum point, the firm earns zero profit, also called the break-even point.

questions.q: The shutdown point of a perfectly competitive firm is the intersection of the marginal cost curve with the:
questions.explanation: The shutdown point is where the AVC curve and the MC curve intersect; below that price the firm does not even cover variable costs.

questions.q: In the short run a firm making losses will continue to operate if price lies between the shutdown point and the zero-profit point.
questions.explanation: In that zone the firm covers its variable costs, so producing gives a smaller loss than shutting down and losing all fixed costs.

questions.q: Which portion of the marginal cost curve forms the short-run supply curve of the firm?
questions.answer: the portion above the average variable cost curve|MC above AVC
questions.explanation: The firm supplies only when price is at or above average variable cost, so its short-run supply curve is the MC curve above AVC.

questions.q: Using cost C = Q^2 + 20Q + 700 and market price Birr 100, the profit-maximizing output is:
questions.explanation: Setting P = MC gives 100 = 2Q + 20, so Q = 40, and profit is Birr 900.

questions.q: Write the chain of equalities that holds in the long-run equilibrium of a perfectly competitive firm and industry.
questions.answer: SMC = LMC = SAC = LAC = P = MR|LMC = LAC = P
questions.explanation: Long-run equilibrium requires LMC = LAC = P at the minimum of LAC, where the full chain SMC = LMC = SAC = LAC = P = MR holds.

questions.q: The short-run supply curve of the competitive industry is obtained from the firms' marginal cost curves by what process?
questions.answer: lateral summation|summing|horizontal summation
questions.explanation: Lateral summation of the portions of firms' short-run MC curves above AVC yields the industry supply curve, which slopes upward.

g11-economics-ue2-t3.overview: A pure monopolist is the only seller of a good with no close substitutes and faces the market demand curve itself. This lesson derives monopoly revenue, short-run equilibrium and the three degrees of price discrimination.
objectives: Define pure monopoly and describe its basic features
Explain why the monopolist's demand curve is the market demand and why MR lies below it
Analyze short-run equilibrium using the TR-TC and MR-MC approaches
Identify the three profit possibilities of a monopolist in the short run
Differentiate first-degree, second-degree and third-degree price discrimination
g11-economics-ue2-t3.simple: A monopoly is at the opposite end of market models from perfect competition: it is the only firm in its industry, the good it sells has no close substitutes and entry by potential rivals is prohibitively difficult. Because it is the sole producer, the monopolist's perceived demand curve is the whole market demand curve, which is downward-sloping, so selling more requires lowering the price. Its marginal revenue always lies below the demand curve and falls twice as fast. The monopolist is a price setter: it chooses the output where MR = MC with MC rising, then charges the demand-curve price. Depending on average cost compared with average revenue it may earn normal, super-normal or zero profits, and it can also practice price discrimination in three degrees to capture consumer surplus.
g11-economics-ue2-t3.detailed:
Features of monopoly. A monopoly firm has no rivals; it is the only firm in its industry, and there are no close substitutes for the good or service it produces. It need not worry about other firms entering because entry by potential rivals is prohibitively difficult. A monopoly does not take the market price as given; it determines its own price, selecting from its demand curve the price that corresponds to the quantity it has chosen in order to earn the maximum possible profit. A firm that sets price based on its output decision is a price setter and possesses monopoly power. In real life pure monopoly is relatively rare, since patent rights exist only for limited periods and it is difficult to keep suppliers from entering.

Demand under monopoly. Each perfectly competitive firm perceives only a tiny slice of the market demand curve, but a monopolist perceives the demand for its product in a market where it is the only producer, so its demand curve is the same as the market demand curve, downward-sloping for most goods. If the monopolist chooses a high level of output it can charge only a relatively low price; if it chooses a low level of output it can charge a higher price. The challenge is to select the price-quantity combination that maximizes profit.

Revenue curves of the monopolist. The monopolist's marginal revenue curve always lies beneath the market demand curve. MR and demand share the same vertical intercept, but as output increases marginal revenue decreases twice as fast as demand, so the horizontal intercept of MR is halfway to the horizontal intercept of demand. The reason MR is less than price is that each additional unit sold pushes down the overall market price, and the lower price then applies to more and more units already sold. Cost curves confront the monopolist in the same typical shapes as a competitive firm: TC, AC and MC have their usual forms, with marginal costs low at small output and rising as output grows. Total revenue, however, differs: it is relatively low at very low output because little is sold, and low again at high output because the large quantity sells only at a low price, so total revenue first rises and then falls.

Short-run equilibrium under monopoly. Short-run equilibrium of the monopolist is the point where profits are maximized or losses minimized. Two approaches apply. In the total revenue - total cost approach, the monopolist produces the output giving the greatest positive difference between TR and TC, or the least negative difference when losses occur; note that the profit-maximizing output is not the revenue-maximizing output, because profits take costs into account while revenue does not. In the marginal approach, two conditions must hold: first, marginal cost is equal to marginal revenue; second, the slope of marginal cost is greater than the slope of marginal revenue at the point of equality. At equilibrium output the monopolist fixes price using the AR (demand) curve; total profit is profit per unit (AR minus AC) multiplied by output. As in perfect competition there are three possibilities: normal profits if AC equals AR, super-normal profits if AC is less than AR, and losses if AC is greater than AR.

Price discrimination and its objective. Price discrimination occurs when a monopolist sells different units of output at different prices, with the objective of maximizing profit or revenue by receiving consumer surplus. The bases for discrimination include consumers' income, geographical location, age, quantity of purchase, relationship with the seller and frequency of visit to the shop. The degree of price discrimination refers to how far a seller can divide the market and extract consumer surplus.

First-degree price discrimination. Under first-degree (perfect or primary) discrimination the seller knows the absolute maximum price, the reservation price, that every consumer is willing to pay, and sells each unit at that maximum price. In this way the entire consumer surplus is transformed into revenue, so profit equals the sum of consumer surplus and producer surplus. The marginal consumer is the one whose reservation price equals the marginal cost; the seller produces more than without discrimination, so there is no deadweight loss, and the demand curve itself becomes the monopolist's MR curve. It is also called take-it-or-leave-it discrimination, because the monopolist offers each consumer the choice of paying the reservation price or getting nothing. In practice it is rare. An example is a medical doctor who knows or guesses a patient's paying capacity and charges the highest fee to the richest patient and the lowest fee to the poorest one.

Second- and third-degree price discrimination. Second-degree (nonlinear) pricing occurs when prices differ according to the number of units bought but not across consumers: every consumer faces the same price schedule, with larger quantities available at lower unit prices, as in quantity discounts. Bulk discounts to industrial customers are common, and pricing may also vary with product quality; airlines offering multiple classes of seats, such as first class and economy, differentiate consumers by preference and capture more consumer surplus. Third-degree price discrimination means charging a different price to different consumer groups and is the most common type, also termed market segmentation. The monopolist divides the market into submarkets that are completely separated and have demands with different elasticities, allocating output so that MC = MR in every market. Railways charging lower fares to senior citizens, and discounts for students at cinemas, museums and historical monuments, are typical examples.

keyTerms.def: A market with a single seller, no close substitutes for the product and entry by rivals prohibitively difficult.
A firm that sets price based on its output decision and therefore possesses monopoly power.
The market demand curve itself, downward-sloping, since the monopolist is the only producer.
Selling different units of output at different prices in order to capture consumer surplus and maximize profit.
The absolute maximum price a consumer is willing to pay for a good; the basis of first-degree discrimination.
The difference between what consumers are willing to pay and what they actually pay, which the discriminating monopolist converts into revenue.
Nonlinear pricing in which price varies with the number of units bought but not across consumers, such as quantity discounts.
Charging different prices to different consumer groups (market segmentation), with MC = MR in each separated submarket.

workedExamples.problem: A monopolist has the cost function C = (1/2)Q^2 and faces the demand curve Q = 12 - P. Find its equilibrium price, output and profit.
workedExamples.given: C = (1/2)Q^2, so MC = Q; demand Q = 12 - P, which rearranges to P = 12 - Q.
workedExamples.formula: First find TR = P x Q, then set MR = MC with MC rising, and read price from the demand curve.
workedExamples.substitution: TR = (12 - Q)Q = 12Q - Q^2, so MR = 12 - 2Q. Setting MR = MC: 12 - 2Q = Q.
workedExamples.calculation: Add 2Q to both sides: 12 = 3Q, so Q = 4 units. Price P = 12 - Q = 8 Birr. TR = 8 x 4 = 32 Birr; TC = (1/2) x 16 = 8 Birr; profit = 32 - 8 = 24 Birr.
workedExamples.answer: Equilibrium output is 4 units, equilibrium price is Birr 8, and monopoly profit is Birr 24 (super-normal profit because AR = 8 exceeds AC = 2).

workedExamples.problem: For the same firm as above, suppose it behaves as if it were in a perfectly competitive industry. What are the competitive price, quantity and profit?
workedExamples.given: Same costs and demand: MC = Q and demand P = 12 - Q.
workedExamples.formula: Competition rule: P = MC.
workedExamples.substitution: Set the demand price equal to MC: 12 - Q = Q, so 2Q = 12 and Q = 6.
workedExamples.calculation: P = 12 - 6 = 6 Birr. TR = 6 x 6 = 36 Birr; TC = (1/2) x 36 = 18 Birr; profit = 36 - 18 = 18 Birr.
workedExamples.answer: Competitive equilibrium is 6 units at Birr 6 with profit 18 Birr; compared with monopoly, output is higher (6 versus 4), price lower (6 versus 8) and profit lower, so the firm would forgo Birr 6 to behave competitively.

workedExamples.problem: A monopoly firm survey of a TR-TC schedule shows, for outputs 1 to 5 units: prices Birr 9, 8, 7, 6, 5; TR Birr 9, 16, 21, 24, 25; TC Birr 5, 10, 13, 19, 27. At which output does the monopolist maximize profit?
workedExamples.given: Prices fall as quantity rises, so TR first rises and then grows slowly, while TC rises steeply.
workedExamples.formula: Total approach: choose the output where TR exceeds TC by the greatest amount.
workedExamples.substitution: Profits = TR - TC = Birr 4, 6, 8, 5, -6 for Q = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
workedExamples.calculation: Profit peaks at Birr 8 when Q = 3. Beyond that, selling extra units pushes the price down so much that TR gains less than TC rises; note that revenue itself keeps rising to Q = 5, showing that revenue-maximizing output is not profit-maximizing output.
workedExamples.answer: The monopolist maximizes profit by producing and selling 3 units, earning Birr 8.

workedExamples.problem: Classify each pricing practice: (a) a doctor charges each patient the highest fee he or she can afford; (b) a soft drink firm gives a discount per bottle for packs of twelve but the same schedule to everyone; (c) a railway charges senior citizens lower fares.
workedExamples.given: Three distinct pricing bases: paying capacity of individuals, quantity bought, and consumer group.
workedExamples.formula: Degree rule: individual reservation prices = first degree; quantity-based = second degree; group-based segmentation = third degree.
workedExamples.substitution: (a) uses the patient's reservation price; (b) varies price with quantity only; (c) charges different prices to separated consumer groups.
workedExamples.calculation: Assign each practice to the degree matching its basis for dividing consumers.
workedExamples.answer: (a) first-degree; (b) second-degree (nonlinear pricing); (c) third-degree (market segmentation).

commonMistakes: Drawing the monopolist's demand curve horizontal like a competitive firm's; the monopoly demand curve is the downward-sloping market demand curve.
Placing the MR curve on or above the demand curve; for a monopolist MR always lies beneath the demand curve and shares only its vertical intercept.
Claiming MR equals price for a monopolist; MR is less than price because extra units force a lower price on all units sold.
Assuming the profit-maximizing output also maximizes revenue; profits take costs into account while revenue does not.
Ignoring the second equilibrium condition: the slope of MC must be greater than the slope of MR at the point of equality.
Reading the equilibrium price from the MR or MC curve instead of from the AR (demand) curve at the chosen output.
Treating all price differences as illegal or as one single practice; discrimination has three distinct degrees with different bases.
applications: Patent rights create temporary monopoly power, but because patents last only limited periods, pure monopoly is rare in the long run.
A doctor who sizes up each patient's paying capacity practices first-degree discrimination, though it is rare because reservation prices are hard to know.
Recognise quantity discounts and different seat classes on flights as second-degree discrimination that captures more consumer surplus.
Discounted museum, cinema and railway fares for students and senior citizens are third-degree discrimination, requiring submarkets kept apart.
Evaluate a monopoly against a competitive outcome: monopoly charges a higher price (Birr 8 versus 6 in the example) and sells less (4 versus 6 units).
Watch for the bases of discrimination around you: income, age, location, quantity bought, relationship with the seller and frequency of visit.
g11-economics-ue2-t3.summary: A pure monopolist is the sole producer with no close substitutes and blocked entry, so it is a price setter whose demand curve is the entire downward-sloping market demand and whose MR lies below demand, falling twice as fast. Short-run equilibrium needs MR = MC with the slope of MC steeper than that of MR, and the price is then read from the AR curve; the outcome can be normal profit, super-normal profit or a loss depending on AC versus AR. To enlarge profit the monopolist may practice price discrimination in three degrees: perfect discrimination using reservation prices, quantity-based nonlinear pricing, and group-based market segmentation.

left.name: Perfect competition
items: Entry eliminates profit in the long run

right.name: Pure monopoly
items: Entry prohibitively difficult; long-run profit possible

steps.label: Find MR = MC
steps.detail: Locate the output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, with MC rising.

steps.label: Choose output
steps.detail: Produce that quantity, called OM in the textbook diagram.

steps.label: Set price from demand
steps.detail: Read the price OP off the AR (demand) curve at that output.

steps.label: Compare AR with AC
steps.detail: AR above AC means super-normal profit per unit; equal means normal; below means loss.

Doctor fees set by each patient's paying capacity

questions.q: For a monopolist, the marginal revenue curve:
questions.explanation: MR always lies beneath the market demand curve; the two share the vertical intercept but MR decreases twice as fast.

questions.q: The demand curve perceived by a monopoly is the same as the market demand curve.
questions.explanation: Since the monopolist is the only producer, its perceived demand curve equals the market demand curve, downward-sloping.

questions.q: A profit-maximizing monopolist determines its output by setting:
options: marginal cost equal to marginal revenue
marginal cost equal to average revenue
questions.explanation: The monopolist sets MC equal to MR (with MC rising) and then charges the demand-curve price; it does not set P = MC.

questions.q: MR - MC = 0 alone is enough to guarantee that a monopolist is maximizing profit.
questions.explanation: A second condition is required: the slope of marginal cost must be greater than the slope of marginal revenue at the point of equality.

questions.q: State the two equilibrium conditions of a monopolist in the short run.
questions.answer: MC = MR and the slope of MC greater than the slope of MR|MC equals MR with MC rising
questions.explanation: First, marginal cost equals marginal revenue; second, the slope of MC exceeds the slope of MR at the equality point.

questions.q: A monopolist whose average cost is less than average revenue at equilibrium earns:
questions.explanation: AC below AR gives super-normal (positive economic) profit; AC equal to AR is normal profit and AC above AR is loss.

questions.q: Under first-degree price discrimination there is no deadweight loss because the marginal consumer's reservation price equals marginal cost.
questions.explanation: Perfect discrimination makes the seller produce up to the consumer whose reservation price equals MC, so more is produced than under uniform monopoly pricing.

questions.q: Quantity discounts, where each consumer faces the same price schedule, are an example of:
questions.explanation: Second-degree (nonlinear) pricing varies price with quantity bought, not across consumers.

questions.q: Which degree of price discrimination is also called market segmentation?
questions.answer: third-degree|third
questions.explanation: Third-degree discrimination divides the market into separated submarkets and charges each group a different price.

questions.q: Explain briefly why a monopolist's marginal revenue is always less than the price.
questions.answer: selling one more unit requires a lower price that applies to all units sold|extra units push down the price on all units
questions.explanation: Each additional unit pushes down the market price, and the lower price applies to more and more units, so added revenue is below price.

questions.q: In the monopoly TR-TC example with prices 9, 8, 7, 6, 5 Birr for 1 to 5 units, how many units maximize profit?
questions.answer: 3 units|three units
questions.explanation: Profit peaks at Birr 8 when 3 units are sold; after that TC rises faster than TR.

g11-economics-ue2-t4.overview: Monopolistic competition combines elements of monopoly and competition: many firms sell distinctive products with free entry. This lesson explains product differentiation, the firm's demand and short-run equilibrium, and the concept of product group.
objectives: Define monopolistic competition and locate it between monopoly and perfect competition
Explain product differentiation, its bases, and the difference between real and spurious differentiation
Describe the demand curve and cost curves of a monopolistically competitive firm
State the two short-run equilibrium conditions of the firm
Explain the concept of industry and product group in differentiated markets
g11-economics-ue2-t4.simple: Monopolistic competition lies between the two extremes of pure competition and monopoly. Many firms compete against each other, but each sells a product that is distinctive in some way, such as different styles of clothing or different kinds of food. Product differentiation may be real, built on differences in specification, inputs or location, or spurious, created by advertising, packaging and brand names. Because its product is distinctive, the firm has some monopoly power and faces a downward-sloping, though relatively elastic, demand curve, but competition from close substitutes keeps its price discretion limited. In the short run the firm maximizes profit where MR = MC with the MR curve cutting the MC curve from below. Since tacit collusion is impossible among many producers, differentiation is the only way to gain market power, and products form a product group rather than an industry.
g11-economics-ue2-t4.detailed:
A mixture of two extremes. The models of perfect competition and pure monopoly represent two ends of the spectrum, but many real markets match neither. Many firms have some control over price, that is, they do not face a perfectly elastic demand curve, yet they are not pure monopolists. Monopolistic competition lies between the two extremes: it captures the mixture of mini-monopoly and tough competition. In real life monopoly is relatively rare, because few suppliers hold sole control of raw materials and patent rights last only limited periods, so elements of monopoly usually exist alongside elements of competition. Typical examples are stores selling different styles of clothing, restaurants or grocery stores selling different kinds of food, and products like golf balls or beer that are similar but differ in public perception because of advertising and brand names.

Product differentiation. Products distinctive in one way or another are called differentiated products. Differentiation is closely related to the variety available: if everyone wore only blue jeans, ate only white bread and drank only tap water, markets for clothing, food and drink would be much closer to perfect competition, so variety of styles, flavours, locations and characteristics creates differentiated products. A general class of product is differentiated if any significant basis exists for distinguishing the good or service of one seller from those of others, whether that basis is real or fancied. Real differentiation occurs when intrinsic characteristics differ, as when some sports shoes are made of synthetic materials and others of leather, or when inputs or the firm's location differ. Spurious or fancied differentiation is established by advertising, differences in packaging, design and simple brand names even when the products are basically the same.

Limited price discretion. Whatever its basis, differentiation intends to persuade consumers to accept a product as unique, rendering the firm a sort of monopoly power, so producers gain some discretion in determining price. The firm is not a price taker. However, it faces keen competition from producers of close substitute products, so its discretion over price is limited. Tacit collusion is virtually impossible when there are many producers, which is why product differentiation is the only way that monopolistically competitive firms can acquire some market power. Two features mark industries with differentiated products: competition among sellers, where entry by more producers reduces the quantity each existing producer sells at any given price, and value in diversity, where consumers gain from the increased variety of products.

Demand and cost curves. A monopolistically competitive firm perceives a demand that is intermediate between monopoly and competition. Its demand curve is not flat but downward-sloping, meaning it can raise price without losing all its customers, or lower price and gain more customers; since there are substitutes available, its demand curve is more elastic than a monopolist's demand curve, where no close substitutes exist. The firm that wants to maximize sales revenue must reduce its price to sell more. The textbook notes that in this market the average revenue curve is U-shaped and marginal revenue falls from left to right, so the firm faces a downward-sloping marginal revenue curve. Cost curves take their usual forms, with average cost U-shaped and marginal cost first falling and then rising.

Short-run equilibrium. The monopolistically competitive firm decides on its profit-maximizing quantity and price in much the same way as a monopolist, choosing a combination along its perceived downward-sloping demand curve. Two marginal conditions must be satisfied in the short run: the necessary or first-order condition, marginal revenue equal to marginal cost (MR = MC), and the supplementary (sufficient) or second-order condition, that the marginal revenue curve cuts the marginal cost curve from the lower side. In the textbook diagram the equilibrium point is E where MR = MC; equilibrium output is OM and price is fixed at OP, and the difference between average cost and average revenue yields a supernormal profit shown by a rectangle for the firm producing that output in the short run.

Industry versus product group. The word industry refers to all firms producing a homogeneous (identical) product. Under monopolistic competition the product is differentiated, so strictly there is no industry but only a group of firms producing similar products: each firm produces a distinct product and is itself an industry. An operational definition of a product group is that the demand for each single product is highly elastic and shifts appreciably when the prices of other products in the group change; that is, products in the group have high price and cross elasticity. For example, a firm producing soap, shampoo and chocolate cannot be called an industry, because those products are not close substitutes.

Toward the long run. If firms in a monopolistically competitive industry earn economic profits, the profits attract entry, and entry continues until profits are driven down to zero in the long run. This follows directly from competition among sellers: as more producers enter, each existing producer sells a smaller quantity at any given price, so the demand curve each firm perceives shifts inward until it is tangential to average cost. Consumers still gain in the long run because value in diversity provides many more varieties than a perfectly competitive market would supply.

keyTerms.def: A market structure between monopoly and perfect competition in which many firms sell differentiated products with free entry.
Any significant basis, real or fancied, for distinguishing the good or service of one seller from those of others.
Differences in product specification, inputs or the firm's location, such as sports shoes made of leather versus synthetic materials.
Differences created by advertising, packaging, design or brand names when the products are basically the same.
The set of firms producing close substitutes, whose products have high price and cross elasticity; under monopolistic competition there is no industry, only a group.
The limited price-setting power a firm gains because buyers perceive its product as unique.
Entry by more producers reduces the quantity each existing producer sells at any given price.
The benefit consumers gain from the increased diversity of differentiated products.

workedExamples.problem: Two sports shoe makers sell shoes of the same size and purpose, but one uses leather and one uses synthetic material, while a third makes identical shoes but wraps them in bright packaging and advertises heavily. Which firms show real and which show spurious differentiation?
workedExamples.given: Maker A: leather shoes; Maker B: synthetic shoes; Maker C: identical shoes plus advertising and packaging.
workedExamples.formula: Rule: differences in specification, inputs or location are real differentiation; advertising, packaging and brand are spurious differentiation.
workedExamples.substitution: A and B differ in intrinsic characteristics (material), which affects the actual product.
workedExamples.calculation: C's product is basically the same; the buyer is merely convinced to buy it through selling activities.
workedExamples.answer: A and B practice real differentiation; C practices spurious (fancied) differentiation.

workedExamples.problem: A restaurant in equilibrium sells 500 plates per month at an average revenue of Birr 32 while its average cost is Birr 24. What profit does it earn in the short run, and what should it expect if rivals imitate its dishes?
workedExamples.given: Output = 500 plates; AR = Birr 32; AC = Birr 24.
workedExamples.formula: Profit per unit = AR - AC; total profit = (AR - AC) x Q.
workedExamples.substitution: Profit per unit = 32 - 24 = Birr 8.
workedExamples.calculation: Total profit = 8 x 500 = Birr 4,000, a supernormal profit because AR is above AC at the MR = MC output. The profit will attract entry by new restaurants, reducing the quantity this restaurant sells at any given price until, in the long run, profits are competed down toward zero.
workedExamples.answer: Short-run supernormal profit is Birr 4,000; entry of imitators will erode it toward zero in the long run.

workedExamples.problem: A firm produces soap, shampoo and chocolate and calls itself the soap industry of the region. Is that name correct?
workedExamples.given: The firm makes three dissimilar products rather than close substitutes.
workedExamples.formula: Rule: an industry is all firms producing a homogeneous product; differentiated close substitutes form a product group.
workedExamples.substitution: Soap, shampoo and chocolate serve different needs and have low cross elasticity.
workedExamples.calculation: A product group requires highly elastic demand for each product that shifts when rivals' prices change; these products do not qualify.
workedExamples.answer: No. Under monopolistic competition there is no industry but only a group of firms producing similar (close-substitute) products, and each firm is itself an industry.

workedExamples.problem: Hair salons in one neighbourhood currently earn economic profits. Predict the price and profit path over the following years.
workedExamples.given: Many sellers of differentiated services; free entry into the market.
workedExamples.formula: Long-run mechanism: entry until economic profits fall to zero.
workedExamples.substitution: New salons open, competing on style, location and price.
workedExamples.calculation: Each salon's perceived demand curve shifts inward as buyers spread over more sellers, moving profit toward zero even though product variety increases.
workedExamples.answer: Entry continues until profits are driven down to zero; salons still earn normal profit, and consumers gain from greater diversity.

commonMistakes: Confusing monopolistic competition with pure monopoly; there are many sellers, and the monopoly element is only each product's distinctiveness.
Saying firms in monopolistic competition sell homogeneous products; the defining feature is differentiated products.
Believing differentiation must be real; advertising and packaging can create spurious differences that buyers value.
Stating only MR = MC and forgetting the second-order condition that MR must cut MC from below.
Expecting supernormal profits to persist; entry by rivals drives profits to zero in the long run.
Calling a firm that makes dissimilar goods (such as soap, shampoo and chocolate) an industry; only close-substitute firms form a product group.
Assuming the demand curve is as inelastic as a monopolist's; the availability of substitutes makes it more elastic.
applications: Explain how shops near a bus station differentiate mainly by location, while shops far away must differentiate by service or product style.
Analyse how advertising makes two chemically similar detergents seem different to buyers, creating spurious differentiation.
Appreciate value in diversity: many restaurants offering different cuisines give consumers choices a single mass supplier could not.
Predict that profitable barbershops attract new entrants, reducing every salon's sales at the old price until only normal profit remains.
Compare bottled water brands that are physically similar yet sold at different prices because brand image builds perceived differences.
Realise why tacit collusion is impossible among many small traders, so each one needs differentiation, not agreement, to gain market power.
g11-economics-ue2-t4.summary: Monopolistic competition mixes mini-monopoly with tough competition: many firms sell differentiated products, whether through real differences in specification, inputs and location or through spurious advertising and branding. Each firm has limited monopoly power, faces a downward-sloping but elastic demand curve, and maximizes short-run profit where MR = MC with MR cutting MC from below; in the long run entry drives profits to zero. Because products are differentiated, there is no industry but only a product group of close substitutes, each firm being an industry of one.

right.name: Competition element
items: Zero profit in the long run

rows: Sports shoes of leather versus synthetic material
Shops near a bus station collect more customers

steps.detail: Set marginal revenue equal to marginal cost (MR = MC).

steps.label: Second-order condition
steps.detail: Confirm MR cuts MC from the lower side (sufficient condition).
