questions.q: Monopolistic competition is best described as a combination of:
questions.explanation: The model captures a mixture of mini-monopoly and tough competition, lying between the two extremes.

questions.q: In the long run, entry of new firms drives the profits of monopolistically competitive firms down to zero.
questions.explanation: Economic profits attract entry until profits are driven to zero because each existing producer sells less at any given price.

questions.q: Product differentiation is a typical feature of:
questions.explanation: Monopolistic competition is defined by many firms selling distinctive products.

questions.q: Define product differentiation and mention two bases on which a firm can build it.
questions.answer: making the product distinctive in physical aspects, location, intangible aspects or perceptions|differentiating by style, location, service or brand image
questions.explanation: Differentiation exists when any significant basis distinguishes a seller's good from others: physical aspects, location, intangibles or perceptions.

questions.q: Differentiation established mainly by advertising, packaging and brand names is called:
questions.explanation: Spurious or fancied differentiation arises when products are basically the same but promotion convinces buyers to prefer one.

questions.q: What do economists call the firms producing close substitute products in monopolistic competition?
questions.answer: product group|a product group
questions.explanation: Since products are differentiated, there is no industry but only a product group with high price and cross elasticity.

questions.q: A monopolistically competitive firm can raise its price without losing all of its customers.
questions.explanation: Its downward-sloping demand means higher price loses only some buyers; but the curve is more elastic than a monopolist's because substitutes exist.

questions.q: State the two marginal conditions for short-run profit maximization under monopolistic competition.
questions.answer: MR = MC and MR cuts MC from below (MC rising)|marginal revenue equals marginal cost with the first cutting the second from the lower side
questions.explanation: The necessary condition is MR = MC; the supplementary condition is that the MR curve cuts the MC curve from the lower side.

questions.q: Why is tacit collusion virtually impossible in monopolistic competition?
questions.explanation: With many producers no firm can coordinate quietly with all rivals, so differentiation, not collusion, is the route to market power.

questions.q: Why is the word industry considered inappropriate under monopolistic competition?
questions.answer: products are differentiated so each firm produces a distinct product and is itself an industry|only a product group of similar firms exists
questions.explanation: An industry requires homogeneous products; under differentiation there is only a group of firms producing similar products.

questions.q: Compared with a monopoly, the demand curve facing a monopolistically competitive firm is:
questions.explanation: Close substitutes make the monopolistic competitor's demand more elastic than the monopolist's, though not perfectly elastic like pure competition.

g11-economics-ue2-t5.overview: Oligopoly is a market of a few dominant sellers whose decisions depend on one another. This lesson contrasts collusive oligopoly, through cartels and price leadership, with non-collusive oligopoly and its Cournot and Bertrand models.
objectives: Define oligopoly and explain strategic interdependence among sellers
Distinguish pure oligopoly from impure (differentiated) oligopoly with examples
Explain collusive oligopoly through cartels and price leadership
Describe non-collusive oligopoly, including the Cournot and Bertrand models
Identify how oligopoly differs from the other market structures
g11-economics-ue2-t5.simple: Oligopoly is a market in which a few dominant sellers sell homogeneous or differentiated products under continuous consciousness of rivals' actions. Because each firm holds a large market share, the actions of one firm affect and are affected by other firms; this is strategic interdependence, so every firm considers rivals' reactions before setting price, output and advertising. Firms selling homogeneous products such as cement, steel or aluminum form pure oligopolies; those selling differentiated products such as cold drinks and automobiles form impure oligopolies. Oligopolists may collude, formally in cartels with a common sales agency or informally through price leadership, to maximize joint profit at a monopoly price. In non-collusive oligopoly each firm competes independently, as in the Cournot (output) and Bertrand (price) models, which produces cut-throat competition, heavy advertising and relative price inflexibility.
g11-economics-ue2-t5.detailed:
Definition and interdependence. Oligopoly is a market in which a few dominant sellers sell differentiated or homogeneous products under continuous consciousness of rivals' actions. Because of the small number of large firms, and hence the large market share of each firm, the actions of one firm affect and are affected by the actions of the other firms in the market; this is known as strategic interdependence. At least some firms have large market shares and can influence the product's price. Oligopolistic firms are aware of their interdependence and always consider rivals' reactions when setting prices, output goals, advertising budgets and other business policies. This contrasts with perfect competition and monopoly, where one can make unambiguous predictions; in oligopoly the large number of possible rival reactions makes it a perplexing market structure, and although perfect competition and pure monopoly are unambiguous, no definite conclusions follow here.

Pure and impure oligopoly. When firms sell homogeneous products such as cement, steel or aluminum they are called pure oligopolies; when firms sell differentiated products such as cold drinks and automobiles they are called impure or differentiated oligopolies. Examples of oligopoly include the pharmaceutical market and the automobile, steel, photographic equipment and beverage (including soft drink) industries. Duopoly is a special case of oligopoly in which two firms operate and have power over the market; the aircraft manufacturers Boeing and Airbus can be considered duopolies. Because every firm aims for strength over rivals, a few powerful competitors emerge that cannot easily be eliminated by other powerful firms, and under these circumstances some firms act together or collude to reap maximum advantage.

Collusive oligopoly. Collusive oligopoly is a form of oligopoly in which competing firms collude to minimize competition and maximize joint profit by reducing the uncertainties arising from rivalry and selling goods and services at a monopoly price. The products sold are homogeneous, so firms know that changing price alone shifts the demand curve because customers can buy the identical product from any of the firms. By deciding not to compete, the firms set a monopoly price and share output so as to maximize joint profit, working in effect as a single firm. Agreements, both explicit (formal) and implicit (informal), are what economists call collusion; firms enter into pricing agreements with each other instead of competing in price wars.

Cartels. The word cartel is used for agreements in which a common sales agency exists that carries out the selling activities of all member firms. Producer firms enter into a formal agreement stating the price and output for all members of the cartel, so the firms jointly fix price and output policy by way of agreements. The common sales agency allocates orders and ensures that members do not undercut one another, turning the group of producers in effect into a single monopoly seller.

Price leadership. When a formal collusive agreement is difficult to launch, oligopolists sometimes operate on informal, tacit collusive agreements. The most common form of informal collusion is price leadership: one dominant firm initiates price changes and the other firms follow or match the change. There is an implicit understanding among the oligopolists to coordinate prices, without any written contract, and all firms gain because uncertainty about rivals' reactions is reduced.

Non-collusive oligopoly. In non-collusive oligopoly the firms are in competition with each other and determine the prices of their products independently, each pursuing its own price and output policy independent of rivals. Because only a few big firms share the market, competition is cut-throat, and firms prefer competition over collusion as a way of maximizing profit; aggressive advertisement develops brand loyalty. Each firm begins with a particular strategy without colluding, and each develops expectations about what rival firms are about to do, considering possible actions and how to react; non-collusive oligopoly is therefore characterized by price inflexibility, since a price change may trigger damaging countermoves. Typical non-collusive models are the Cournot model, in which competitors offer a homogeneous product and compete on the amount of output produced, independently and concurrently, and the Bertrand model, in which few firms produce identical goods at a constant marginal cost, treat competitors' prices as fixed when setting their own prices, and end up producing the competitive level of output. Oligopolists may also turn to non-price competition such as product development and investment in research and development to distinguish their products and gain a competitive edge.

keyTerms.def: A market in which a few dominant sellers sell homogeneous or differentiated products under continuous consciousness of rivals' actions.
The condition in which each firm's actions affect and are affected by the actions of the other firms because each holds a large market share.
An oligopoly whose firms sell homogeneous products, such as cement, steel or aluminum.
An oligopoly whose firms sell differentiated products, such as cold drinks and automobiles.
A special case of oligopoly in which exactly two firms operate and have power over the market, such as Boeing and Airbus in large aircraft.
Explicit (formal) or implicit (informal) agreements among oligopolists to cooperate instead of competing, so as to maximize joint profit.
A formal collusive agreement in which a common sales agency performs the selling activities of all member firms who jointly fix price and output.
Informal, tacit collusion in which one dominant firm initiates price changes and the other firms follow or match them.

workedExamples.problem: Classify these sellers: (a) three cement producers selling identical cement; (b) four soft drink companies each marketing its own heavily advertised brand; (c) the only two makers of large commercial aircraft.
workedExamples.given: (a) few sellers + homogeneous product; (b) few sellers + branded differentiated product; (c) exactly two powerful sellers.
workedExamples.formula: Rule: homogeneous product among few firms = pure oligopoly; differentiated product = impure oligopoly; two firms = duopoly.
workedExamples.substitution: Cement units are indistinguishable to buyers, while each soft drink brand carries its own perception.
workedExamples.calculation: Boeing and Airbus form a special case with exactly two firms, so it is named duopoly.
workedExamples.answer: (a) pure oligopoly; (b) impure (differentiated) oligopoly; (c) duopoly, a special case of oligopoly.

workedExamples.problem: In a market with three large breweries, beer sales fall whenever any firm changes price on its own, because uncertainty about rivals causes price wars. The firms instead sign a formal contract appointing one common sales agency to set price and allocate output. Which oligopoly arrangement is this?
workedExamples.given: A formal written agreement with one common sales agency for all members; products are homogeneous.
workedExamples.formula: Rule: formal agreement + common sales agency + jointly fixed price and output = cartel.
workedExamples.substitution: The agency carries out the selling activities of all member firms, so consumers face one monopoly-like price.
workedExamples.calculation: Joint profit is maximized as if the breweries were a single monopoly seller, replacing cut-throat rivalry.
workedExamples.answer: A cartel, the formal (explicit) type of collusive oligopoly.

workedExamples.problem: In the same market the firms cannot meet openly to agree, so the largest firm quietly announces a price increase and the other two match it within days. Which arrangement is this now?
workedExamples.given: No formal contract; one dominant firm moves first and others follow.
workedExamples.formula: Rule: informal tacit agreement + dominant firm initiating price changes followed by others = price leadership.
workedExamples.substitution: The dominant brewery initiates each price change and the followers match it.
workedExamples.calculation: Coordination is achieved through an implicit understanding, avoiding both a formal cartel and a price war.
workedExamples.answer: Price leadership, the most common form of informal collusion.

workedExamples.problem: Two firms sell identical bolts with constant marginal cost. Firm 1 lowers its quotation treating Firm 2's price as given; Firm 2 responds by treating Firm 1's new price as fixed and undercuts. Predict the long-run direction of this non-collusive interaction.
workedExamples.given: Identical products, constant marginal cost, and each firm setting price independently while taking the rival's price as fixed.
workedExamples.formula: Bertrand logic: competing in price with identical products drives price toward the competitive level.
workedExamples.substitution: Each undercut gains the whole market, so rivals keep matching until price approaches marginal cost.
workedExamples.calculation: The outcome approaches the competitive level of output, unlike Cournot's output competition.
workedExamples.answer: Bertrand rivalry: prices converge downward toward marginal cost and output toward the competitive level.

commonMistakes: Believing an oligopolist can set its price without regard to rivals; strategic interdependence forces every firm to anticipate rivals' reactions.
Mixing up pure oligopoly (homogeneous goods like cement and steel) with impure oligopoly (differentiated goods like automobiles and soft drinks).
Assuming collusive oligopoly means intense competition; collusion exists to minimize competition and establish a monopoly-like price.
Confusing cartels, which are formal agreements run through a common sales agency, with price leadership, which is informal and led by a dominant firm.
Expecting definite, unambiguous conclusions from oligopoly models the way one can for perfect competition or monopoly.
Forgetting duopoly is itself a special case of oligopoly, not a separate structure outside it.
Overlooking non-price competition such as product development and research and development, which firms use instead of cutting prices.
applications: View a national cement or steel market with few large producers of a homogeneous product as a pure oligopoly.
Notice that soft drink producers compete mainly through aggressive advertising that builds brand loyalty, a hallmark of non-collusive oligopoly.
Evaluate why few large firms signing contracts to fix a common price raise joint profit but reduce uncertainty only for themselves, hurting buyers.
Recognise price leadership in practice: when the dominant firm announces a price change for fertiliser or fuel distribution, smaller rivals quickly match it.
Apply strategic interdependence when advising a firm: before cutting price, predict how each rival will respond and whether a price war follows.
Observe duopoly worldwide in large commercial aircraft, where Boeing and Airbus together hold power over the market.
g11-economics-ue2-t5.summary: Oligopoly is a market of a few dominant sellers, homogeneous or differentiated, bound together by strategic interdependence: each firm must consider rivals' reactions before setting price, output and advertising. Under collusive oligopoly firms minimize rivalry and maximize joint profit through formal cartels with a common sales agency or through informal price leadership by a dominant firm, while under non-collusive oligopoly each firm competes independently, as modelled by Cournot (output) and Bertrand (price), producing cut-throat competition and price inflexibility. Duopoly, in which two firms like Boeing and Airbus rule the market, is a special case of oligopoly.

config.title: Types of Oligopoly by Product and Number

questions.q: Which of the following is a unique characteristic of oligopoly?
options: The use of advertising and product development
Mutual interdependence among firms in the industry
questions.explanation: Strategic, mutual interdependence among the few dominant firms is the distinctive feature of oligopoly.

questions.q: Oligopolistic firms are aware of their interdependence and consider rivals' reactions when setting prices, output goals and advertising budgets.
questions.explanation: Continuous consciousness of rivals' actions is part of the definition of oligopoly.

questions.q: Under conditions of oligopoly, firms may collude in order to:
options: avoid the uncertainty of rivals' reactions and enlarge market power
force the government to set prices
questions.explanation: Collusion minimizes competition, reduces the uncertainties of rivalry and lets firms sell at a monopoly price for maximum joint profit.

questions.q: Which statement about oligopoly is FALSE?
options: Entry into the market is difficult
Each firm makes decisions without regard for the actions of other firms
Game-type reasoning is needed to analyse firm behaviour
Firms often have an incentive to collude
questions.explanation: Exactly the opposite is true: every decision is made with continuous consciousness of rivals' actions.

questions.q: Price leadership is a form of informal collusion in which one dominant firm initiates price changes and the others follow or match them.
questions.explanation: When a formal agreement is difficult, oligopolists use implicit, tacit agreements, the most common being price leadership.

questions.q: Define strategic interdependence.
questions.answer: the actions of one firm affect and are affected by the actions of the other firms because each has a large market share|firms' decisions depend on rivals' expected reactions
questions.explanation: Because the market is held by a few large firms, each firm's actions influence rivals, which is known as strategic interdependence.

questions.q: Which non-collusive model assumes homogeneous products and independent, simultaneous competition on quantity of output?
questions.answer: Cournot model|Cournot
questions.explanation: The Cournot model describes competitors offering a homogeneous product who compete on the amount of output produced.

questions.q: In the Bertrand model each firm sets price while treating competitors' prices as fixed; as a result the market ends up:
options: producing the monopoly level of output
producing the competitive level of output
questions.explanation: Bertrand firms compete in price, and the outcome is the competitive level of output, unlike Cournot's output competition.

questions.q: Give the name for the special case of oligopoly in which exactly two firms operate and hold power over the market.
questions.answer: duopoly
questions.explanation: Duopoly is a two-firm oligopoly; Boeing and Airbus are cited as examples.

questions.q: Why do non-colluding oligopolists prefer non-price competition such as product development?
questions.answer: because price cuts trigger rival countermoves and price wars, so firms use advertising and R and D to gain market share|prices are inflexible, so rivalry shifts to product development
questions.explanation: With strategic interdependence and price inflexibility, firms invest in research and development and product development to gain a competitive edge instead of cutting price.

questions.q: Firms selling homogeneous products such as cement, steel or aluminum are called what type of oligopoly?
questions.answer: pure oligopoly|pure
questions.explanation: Homogeneous-product oligopolies are pure oligopolies; differentiated-product ones are impure.
